title: Sakhi AI
tagline: Voice-first AI companion concept for rural women's health & safety
shortDescription: A voice-first conversational assistant designed to give rural women accessible health information, safety guidance, and emergency support without requiring literacy or a stable internet connection.
problemStatement: Many rural women lack easy access to trusted health information and safety resources. Low literacy, language barriers, and limited smartphone proficiency make most existing digital tools unreachable, and there's often no accessible, judgment-free system to turn to in a crisis moment.
solution: A voice-based conversational agent that lets users speak naturally instead of typing, aimed at working on low-bandwidth connections and routing urgent situations toward local support resources.
impact: Built as a voice-first assistant concept; specific usage numbers are not independently verifiable from the project sources currently available and are intentionally left out rather than estimated.
architecture: Mobile frontend → backend API → conversational AI layer → speech-to-text / text-to-speech → database layer for storing and retrieving knowledge used in responses.
features: Voice-based interaction instead of text input
Designed for low-bandwidth / low-connectivity conditions
Emergency escalation path toward local support resources
Anonymized health Q&A grounded in a curated knowledge base
Conversation history with privacy-conscious local storage
challenges: Designing voice UX for users with little to no prior smartphone experience
Keeping response latency low on constrained connections
Handling sensitive health and safety queries responsibly
lessonsLearned: Voice UX requires different design principles than text — silence handling and confirmation loops matter a lot
Safety-related guardrails need to be context-aware rather than simple keyword matching

title: IT Ops Intelligence
tagline: AI-assisted IT operations intelligence for incident detection, SLA management, and evidence-based root-cause analysis
shortDescription: A real, containerized IT operations command center: four live FastAPI microservices are monitored end-to-end, with automatic incident detection against SLA thresholds, a rule-based root-cause analysis engine, and an optional LLM explanation layer that a human must verify before it's treated as fact.
problemStatement: When services fail, on-call teams need to detect the failure from real signals (not customer complaints), track it against an SLA so nothing silently blows past its deadline, and find the root cause fast enough to fix it in time. Manual dashboards and ad-hoc log-grepping don't scale past a handful of services, and pure ML-based anomaly detection is often a black box that's hard to defend to a manager or auditor.
solution: A Central Platform polls four real backend microservices (auth, orders, payments, db-proxy) on a configurable interval, reduces their Prometheus metrics into error rate, latency, and availability, and opens an incident with calculated SLA deadlines the moment a threshold is breached. From there, a rule-based RCA engine evaluates the incident's correlated metrics and logs and proposes a root-cause category with a confidence level and cited evidence. Only after that deterministic result exists can an operator optionally request an LLM explanation, which is grounded strictly in the rule engine's own evidence, explicitly refuses to guess when the evidence is insufficient, degrades gracefully to a rule-based summary if no API key is configured or the call fails, and is stored as unverified until a human operator reviews and verifies it. Every state-changing action is written to an audit log.
impact: Verified end-to-end rather than just described: 63 of 63 automated tests pass (55 unit, 8 integration against a real PostgreSQL instance), plus a Postman collection with negative cases and a real Locust load-test run. A self-audit of the project surfaced and fixed real defects — including an unauthenticated fault-injection endpoint, a silently hard-coded SLA threshold, and a stored-XSS vector in the dashboard — each with a documented reproduce-to-regression-test trail.
architecture: Frontend (HTML/CSS/JS dashboard) → Central Platform (FastAPI: incident, SLA, services, and conversion routers, plus a background poll loop) → 4 backend microservices, each exposing /health, Prometheus-format /metrics, and token-authenticated /admin fault-injection endpoints → PostgreSQL (8 tables: users, services, incidents, logs, metrics, sla_rules, recommendations, audit_logs) → Prometheus (scrapes all 4 services every 10s) → Grafana dashboard. RCA flow: correlated metric/log evidence → rule-based RCA engine → structured result (category, confidence, cited evidence) → optional LLM explanation (grounded in that evidence only) → human verification → operator decision, all captured in the audit trail.
features: Real-time polling of 4 live microservices' /health and Prometheus /metrics endpoints
Automatic incident creation on error-rate, latency, or availability threshold breaches
SLA engine that calculates response/resolution deadlines and flags breaches automatically
Rule-based, fully explainable RCA engine — every conclusion traces to a specific evidence item
Optional LLM explanation layer with grounded prompting, an explicit 'undetermined' refusal path, and graceful fallback when no API key is configured or the call fails
Human verification workflow before any AI-generated explanation is treated as fact
Full audit trail on every incident lifecycle action (acknowledge, resolve, verify)
Legacy incident CSV conversion: validate, dedupe, and load, with a per-row conversion log
Token-authenticated fault-injection admin endpoints for realistic failure drills
Prometheus scrape config and a Grafana dashboard whose PromQL queries match this project's real metric names
One-command Docker Compose deployment across all 8 services
challenges: Distinguishing a symptom category (e.g. 'service outage') from the true underlying cause — a failure-injection drill showed the rule engine correctly flagging availability loss while the real cause (a bad deploy breaking health checks too) still required human judgment

An ambiguous-evidence drill exposed a real RCA misclassification (a DB-timeout logged without the exact keywords the rule expected), fixed and covered with a dedicated regression test rather than papered over
A missing runtime dependency (python-multipart) caused the entire app to fail at import time only when FastAPI introspected the upload route — a startup-time failure disguised as a request-time one

A self-audit found the /admin/* fault-injection endpoints across all 4 services had zero authentication, and that dashboard fields (including CSV-sourced incident titles) were inserted via unescaped innerHTML — both fixed and regression-tested
lessonsLearned: Rule-based RCA is more defensible and explainable than ML at this scale — there isn't enough labeled failure data to train a real model, and every conclusion needs to trace back to cited evidence, not a black-box score

An LLM layer on top of a deterministic engine is only safe with hard grounding: constrain the prompt to the rule engine's own evidence, give it an explicit refusal path for 'undetermined', and make human verification part of the workflow rather than optional
Auditing your own project honestly — correcting a previously wrong test count and disclosing the error rather than quietly fixing it — surfaces real defects that a first pass of documentation missed
Config validated statically (YAML/JSON parsing, PromQL metric-name cross-checks) is not the same claim as 'run live' — worth being explicit about which is which rather than blurring the two

title: LRU Cache
tagline: A caching layer built around LRU eviction and distributed key lookup
shortDescription: A caching layer concept for URL resolution and web content, combining an in-memory LRU tier with a persistent backing store, aimed at fast lookups and controlled invalidation.
problemStatement: Systems like URL shorteners, crawlers, or edge nodes need a caching layer that handles frequent key lookups with low latency and predictable invalidation, without the overhead of a general-purpose distributed cache.
solution: A purpose-built caching design using an in-memory LRU cache as a fast first tier backed by a persistent store, with TTL-based expiry and an invalidation path for updates.
impact: Specific throughput and latency figures are not independently verifiable from the project sources currently available and have been left out rather than estimated.
architecture: Client requests → in-memory LRU cache (tier 1) → persistent backing store (tier 2) → TTL expiry → invalidation path for updated keys.
features: In-memory LRU eviction policy for the hot cache tier
Two-tier design: fast in-memory cache backed by a persistent store
TTL-based automatic expiry
Invalidation path for updated or stale keys
challenges: Tuning eviction and tier-promotion behavior under concurrent access
Deciding write-through vs write-back trade-offs between the two cache tiers
lessonsLearned: Two-tier caches require a deliberate write-through vs write-back choice — write-back is faster but risks data loss on failure

title: Mini Database Engine
tagline: A relational database built from scratch in Python
shortDescription: A from-scratch implementation of a relational database engine covering SQL parsing, indexing, a buffer pool, write-ahead logging, and a query planner — built to understand how databases actually work internally.
problemStatement: Most developers use databases as black boxes. Building one from scratch is a direct way to understand query optimization, storage internals, concurrency control, and crash recovery.
solution: A Python implementation with a hand-written SQL parser, a B-tree index structure, a buffer pool with LRU eviction, a write-ahead log for crash recovery, and a query planner with join ordering.
impact: Specific benchmark results and course-adoption claims are not independently verifiable from the project sources currently available and have been left out rather than estimated. The engine supports SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, and index-based scans.
architecture: SQL Parser (recursive descent) → AST → Query Planner → Execution Engine → Buffer Pool Manager (LRU) → B-tree Storage Engine → Write-Ahead Log → Crash Recovery Module → file-based storage pages.
features: Hand-written recursive descent SQL parser
B-tree index with split/merge and range scan support
Buffer pool manager with LRU eviction policy
Write-ahead logging for crash recovery
Cost-based query planner with join ordering
Simple SQL shell for interactive querying
challenges: Implementing B-tree split propagation correctly
Designing a WAL format that supports both redo and undo operations efficiently
Building a cost estimator without real statistics collection infrastructure
Handling page boundary edge cases in variable-length record storage
lessonsLearned: B-tree rebalancing is conceptually simple but edge cases require exhaustive testing
WAL is a relatively elegant crash recovery mechanism compared to shadow paging
Query planner cost models are inaccurate without real data statistics

title: Hallucination Detection System
tagline: LLM output verification via claim decomposition and entailment checking
shortDescription: A pipeline that detects and flags likely hallucinations in LLM outputs using claim decomposition and knowledge-grounded entailment checking, designed as a middleware layer for LLM-backed systems.
problemStatement: LLMs can confidently generate factually incorrect information, which is risky for high-stakes use cases. Manual review doesn't scale, and simple similarity-based detection methods miss subtle fabrications.
solution: A claim decomposition pipeline that breaks LLM responses into atomic facts, verifies each against retrieved source documents using an NLI model, and returns a hallucination assessment with per-claim attribution.
impact: Specific precision/recall benchmark numbers and production usage figures are not independently verifiable from the project sources currently available and have been left out rather than estimated.
architecture: LLM output → claim decomposer → retrieval module → NLI verifier → entailment scorer → aggregator → hallucination report with confidence → middleware response interceptor.
features: Atomic claim decomposition from free-form LLM text
Per-claim source retrieval and NLI verification
Hallucination classification (fabrication, exaggeration, contradiction)
Confidence-calibrated output scores
Batch mode for post-hoc evaluation of historical outputs
challenges: Decomposing compound claims without losing context or creating false negatives
Keeping end-to-end latency low enough for near-real-time interception
Handling partial hallucinations where only part of a claim is fabricated
lessonsLearned: Claim granularity is an important tuning factor — too coarse misses fabrications, too fine creates noise
Attribution (which source contradicts which claim) is more useful to users than a single aggregate score

title: Disaster Relief Coordination Portal
tagline: Planned real-time coordination platform for disaster relief teams
shortDescription: A planned real-time coordination platform intended to help disaster relief organizations track resource needs, volunteer deployment, and supply logistics, designed to work offline-first in connectivity-degraded disaster zones.
problemStatement: During disaster response, coordination between NGOs, government agencies, and volunteers can break down due to fragmented communication, no shared resource visibility, and tools that fail when internet infrastructure is damaged.
solution: Intended to be a PWA with offline-first architecture using local sync and conflict-free data merging, with real-time updates when connectivity is available and a map-based resource visualization layer.
impact: Not yet built — no implementation, deployment, or usage claims apply yet.
architecture: Planned: React PWA (offline-first) with local storage and background sync → real-time server updates when connected → database with geospatial support → map-based UI layer.
features: Planned offline-first support with conflict-free data sync
Planned real-time map of resource needs and volunteer positions
Planned role-based access for NGOs, government, and volunteers
Planned resource request and fulfillment workflow with status tracking
challenges: Designing sync that will work correctly with geospatial data types
Designing UX that will work for non-technical users under stress
Planning for reliability over degraded or intermittent networks

title: GitHub Analytics Tool
tagline: Planned developer productivity analytics from GitHub data
shortDescription: A planned developer analytics tool intended to ingest GitHub activity across repositories and surface productivity patterns, code quality trends, and collaboration insights, with a natural-language query interface envisioned as a future addition.
problemStatement: Engineering managers often lack objective, data-driven insight into team productivity and collaboration patterns. Manual analysis of GitHub data is time-consuming.
solution: Intended to be an ETL pipeline that ingests GitHub events via webhooks and the REST API, stores them in a queryable schema, and exposes a dashboard with drill-down analytics.
impact: Not yet built — no implementation, deployment, or usage claims apply yet.
architecture: Planned: GitHub Webhooks/REST API → ingestion service → database → analytics API → React dashboard.
features: Planned ingestion of commits, PRs, reviews, and issues
Planned contribution and review-cycle-time analytics
Planned collaboration graph across teams
Planned natural-language querying over the collected data
challenges: Handling GitHub API rate limits during historical backfill
Designing metrics that are meaningful without incentivizing gaming
Choosing a schema that scales for multi-repo, multi-org data

title: Interactive Power BI / Data Analytics Dashboard
shortDescription: A planned interactive Power BI dashboard project intended to showcase data modeling, DAX measures, and business-facing reporting on top of a cleaned, structured dataset.
problemStatement: Raw business data is rarely analysis-ready — it needs cleaning, modeling, and a well-designed schema before it can support interactive, drillable reporting for decision-makers.
solution: Not yet built. Will explore the full BI workflow: Power Query-based data cleaning and ETL, a star-schema data model with fact and dimension tables, DAX measures and calculated columns (including CALCULATE(), SUM(), AVERAGE(), COUNT(), and time intelligence), and an interactive report with slicers, filters, drill-downs, and KPI cards.

title: Custom Data Structure Library
tagline: Planned library of advanced data structures with benchmarks
shortDescription: A planned from-scratch library of advanced data structures in Python and C++, each intended to include complexity analysis, randomized correctness testing, and benchmark comparisons against standard library equivalents.
problemStatement: Standard library data structures are optimized for general use but suboptimal for specific access patterns. Building alternatives from scratch is intended to deepen understanding of when to reach for something other than the default.
solution: Not yet built. Planned to include structures such as skip lists, Fibonacci heaps, splay trees, and persistent data structures, each with randomized correctness tests and micro-benchmarks.
impact: Not yet built — no implementation, benchmark, or adoption claims apply yet.
architecture: Planned: each data structure as a standalone module — interface definition → implementation → property-based randomized tests → benchmark harness → complexity analysis documentation.
features: Planned skip list, Fibonacci heap, and splay tree implementations
Planned persistent (path-copying) tree variant
Planned property-based randomized correctness testing
Planned micro-benchmarks against standard library equivalents
challenges: Implementing Fibonacci heap decrease-key without introducing heap-order bugs
Designing persistent data structures that share structure efficiently
Benchmarking in a way that controls for CPU frequency scaling and cache warmup
